m2.buyer.a1.action: Habitual Starbucks app users who experienced significant mobile order delays (>8 minutes) at pilot stores in January will begin February by trying competitor mobile apps, drawn by promotions like the Dutch Bros $1 Order Ahead offer. Their return to Starbucks is now contingent on the quality of the competitor's service.

m2.buyer.a2.action: In-store café visitors at the pilot Starbucks locations, having experienced shorter and more predictable wait times in January, will reinforce this behavior in February. We will choose these locations more frequently for occasions that value a reliable in-store experience.

m2.buyer.a3.action: Time-pressed commuters will continue to check the Starbucks app before committing, but will more readily divert to Dutch Bros or Dunkin' on any morning the quoted pickup time creates a risk of being late.

m2.dunkin.a1.action: Launch a $1 discount breakfast bundle offer through the Dunkin app at all 15 consenting franchise stores near the Starbucks pilot cafés during the February 2027 morning peak (7-10 a.m. weekdays).

m2.dunkin.a2.action: Allocate $12,000 of the $20,000 monthly budget to incremental morning labor to improve order fulfillment speed and reduce wait times, aiming to compete with Starbucks' capacity-aware mobile pickup slots.

m2.dunkin.a3.action: Use $8,000 for targeted local app advertising and promotions to drive repeat visits and encourage use of the $1 discount bundle, with monitoring of basket contribution and repeat customer behavior.

m2.dunkin.a4.action: Set a stop rule to discontinue the discount offer at any store where the store-level contribution margin worsens after one month.

m2.dutch.a1.action: Continue to allocate $15,000/month for incremental morning labor at 12 shops near Starbucks pilot cafés.

m2.dutch.a2.action: Continue to allocate $15,000/month for geo-targeted $1 Order Ahead app offer for new/lapsed users at 12 shops near Starbucks pilot cafés.

m2.home.a1.action: Continue the 20% peak café capacity reservation and mobile order admission limits in the 50 pilot cafés through February 2027, maintaining the current weekday 07:00–10:00 window.

m2.home.a2.action: Within the pilot, begin a controlled test in 10 of the 50 cafés: dynamically release any unused reserved café capacity to mobile orders if, after the first 60 minutes of peak, café demand is tracking below the 20% allocation (e.g., if less than 15% of capacity has actually been used for café orders by 08:00, release half of the remaining reserved slots for mobile pickup for the rest of the peak window).

board.evidence_status: Public research through 2026-09-12. Future actions and outcomes are a model simulation. No actual pilot store or customer records are supplied.
board.measurement_rule: Null means unmeasured. Keep real measurement fields null and complete observed sample counts at zero without sourced operating records. Put hypothetical estimates in separately named simulated_* fields with assumptions, never in observed fields. Maintain a concise public_strategy_history of observable implemented actions and consequences so later players can adapt. Do not publish private budgets, dossiers or unseen internal intentions. Advance calendar_period to the end of the current month.
board.public_market_context: Starbucks is investing in coffeehouse service, staffing and Smart Queue while US transactions are growing. Dutch Bros offers drive-through beverages and Order Ahead at participating shops. Dunkin offers coffee-and-food value and mobile ordering through a franchise network. Some morning purchases can shift to home preparation or disappear. Local overlaps and customer segments in this exercise are assumptions.

public_strategy_history.customer: Habitual Starbucks app users attempt mobile orders but abandon if quoted slot is >8 minutes late; after two such failures in a week, shift routine to a competitor for the rest of the month. Time-pressed commuters check app and divert if a delay risks lateness. In-store café visitors continue, with increased visit frequency if wait times improve.
public_strategy_history.dunkin: Launched $6 breakfast Meal Deal with coffee and food in 15 local franchise stores near pilot cafés; promoted via app/local channels; monitored basket economics and set rule to discontinue if store-level contribution worsens.
public_strategy_history.dutch_bros: Allocated $15,000/month for incremental morning labor and $15,000/month for geo-targeted $1 Order Ahead app offer for new/lapsed users at 12 shops near pilot cafés.
public_strategy_history.starbucks: Implemented 20% capacity reservation for in-café orders in 50 pilot cafés during weekday 7–10 a.m.; mobile pickup slots limited accordingly. Instrumented pilot and comparison cafés for order attempts, slot offers, completions, and staffing.

criteria.condition: The baseline-adjusted reduction in peak café order-to-handoff p90 wait is less than 20 percent by move two across at least forty complete pilot/comparison store pairs
criteria.observable: adjusted_cafe_wait_reduction_pct; equally weighted store-pair changes in p90 wait, comparing peak weekday windows before and after the pilot; complete_store_pairs >= 40
criteria.threshold: Below 20% reduction; fewer than 40 complete pairs or missing baseline/wait evidence is unevaluated

criteria.condition: Adjusted daily contribution per pilot café after lost orders, substitution between channels and incremental staffing is negative by move three across at least forty complete store pairs
criteria.observable: incremental_daily_contribution_usd after matched-store baseline adjustment, including all channels and added labor; complete_store_pairs >= 40
criteria.threshold: Below $0 per café per day; incomplete transaction or cost evidence is unevaluated

criteria.condition: Thirty-day repeat purchase among baseline mobile customers falls by more than three percentage points relative to the comparison-cohort change by move three
criteria.observable: mobile_repeat_change_pp; compare baseline-defined cohorts across all Starbucks purchase channels, with at least 1000 customers per arm and complete 30-day follow-up
criteria.threshold: Below -3 percentage points; incomplete cohorts or missing follow-up is unevaluated

decision.launch_period: January 2027; a proposed experiment, not an announced Starbucks policy
decision.offer: Capacity-aware mobile pickup slots with a protected café-order allocation from 7–10 a.m. on weekdays
decision.pricing: Keep beverage prices unchanged; assumed $3 contribution per incremental or lost transaction before added staffing, not a reported company figure
decision.scope: 50 pilot cafés and 50 comparison cafés; reserve 20% of measured 15-minute capacity for café orders at peak; no automatic transfer of the policy to other stores
decision.segment: 50 US company-operated cafés with nearby Dutch Bros and Dunkin alternatives, paired with 50 comparison cafés
decision.statement: Pilot peak-time mobile-order admission limits in 50 US Starbucks cafés during January–March 2027, reserving 20% of measured production capacity for café orders and offering later pickup slots when the mobile allocation is full.

capabilities: Choose a brand, channel, later time, home preparation or no purchase based on the public offer (b2, b7, b8).
State contingent choices separately for commuters, habitual app users and café visitors, without inventing population shares (b3, b4, b5, b6).
constraints: Each occasion has its own explicit time and spending ceiling; do not average them into a universal customer (b4, b5, b6).
No measured segment weights, switching probability or real participant testimony exists (b1, b3, b8).

Loyalty friction exists, but its monetary value and prevalence are unknown.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed economics: $3 contribution per incremental or lost transaction before additional staffing. Assume fully loaded incremental labor costs $30/hour for sensitivity calculations. Two added hours cost $60/store/day and require 20 genuinely incremental transactions to break even before other costs. No actual store margins, baselines or demand elasticities are supplied.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed management problem: The operations lead is accountable for café service and labor spend; the digital lead for reliable pickup and repeat behavior; the finance lead for all-channel contribution. Optimizing one channel at another’s expense is not success. These are role tensions constructed for the game, not testimony from executives.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed information rights: The team can instrument its own order attempts, offered pickup slots, completed orders, refunds, staffing hours and baseline-linked repeat purchases; it cannot see rivals’ transaction logs or know where a rejected mobile user ultimately buys. Available instrumentation is a capability, not already collected evidence.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed decision rules: By round two seek at least a 20% adjusted café p90 wait reduction across 40 complete pairs. By round three require nonnegative daily contribution and no worse than a 3pp adjusted repeat decline with 1,000 complete customers per arm. Missing evidence cannot pass these gates.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

incentives: Restore a credible coffeehouse visit without sacrificing digital convenience (h1, h4).
Defend positive transaction momentum while earning back added labor through all-channel contribution (h2, h3, h6).
Make a reversible operational choice before the March decision deadline (h5, h9).
red_lines: Do not invent operating measurements or declare the economics gate passed from a better wait-time story alone (h6, h9).
Do not promise a national rollout or exceed the staffing cap (h5).

actions: Habitual Starbucks app users who experienced significant mobile order delays (>8 minutes) at pilot stores in January will begin February by trying competitor mobile apps, drawn by promotions like the Dutch Bros $1 Order Ahead offer. Their return to Starbucks is now contingent on the quality of the competitor's service.

In-store café visitors at the pilot Starbucks locations, having experienced shorter and more predictable wait times in January, will reinforce this behavior in February. We will choose these locations more frequently for occasions that value a reliable in-store experience.

Time-pressed commuters will continue to check the Starbucks app before committing, but will more readily divert to Dutch Bros or Dunkin' on any morning the quoted pickup time creates a risk of being late.
expected_responses: We expect Starbucks to see a mixed signal from the pilot: happier in-store customers and higher in-store sales, but a potential drop in mobile order volume and the loss of some previously loyal app users to competitors. They might adjust the 20% capacity reservation.

We expect Dutch Bros and Dunkin' to see a measurable increase in new customer trials and mobile orders at their locations near the pilot stores. They will likely continue their promotions to try and make our new habits stick.
content.rationale: My choices are a direct reaction to the new reality at the pilot Starbucks stores and the offers from competitors. The Starbucks policy has improved the experience for one type of visit (in-café) at the expense of another (peak-time mobile orders). For those of us who rely on the app for a quick pickup, the new system can be unreliable. When competitors like Dutch Bros and Dunkin' make it easy and cheap to try their service, it's a logical time to explore new routines. Conversely, when I actually want to sit in a café, the pilot stores have become more pleasant and reliable, so I'll go there more often for that purpose.
resource_commitments: Attention and Time: We are willing to spend the time to download a new app and learn a new ordering routine if the incentive is strong enough (like a $1 offer) and our current routine is broken.
Daily Spend: Our daily budget for coffee and breakfast will be reallocated to the brand that best meets the needs of a specific morning's occasion—be it speed, value, or in-store experience.

actions: Launch a $1 discount breakfast bundle offer through the Dunkin app at all 15 consenting franchise stores near the Starbucks pilot cafés during the February 2027 morning peak (7-10 a.m. weekdays).

Allocate $12,000 of the $20,000 monthly budget to incremental morning labor to improve order fulfillment speed and reduce wait times, aiming to compete with Starbucks' capacity-aware mobile pickup slots.
Use $8,000 for targeted local app advertising and promotions to drive repeat visits and encourage use of the $1 discount bundle, with monitoring of basket contribution and repeat customer behavior.
Set a stop rule to discontinue the discount offer at any store where the store-level contribution margin worsens after one month.
expected_responses: Starbucks may maintain or tighten their 20% capacity reservation for in-café orders, possibly improving mobile pickup slot availability or further optimizing staffing.
Dutch Bros may respond by increasing their geo-targeted $1 Order Ahead offers or adding incremental labor to maintain competitive speed and value.
Some customers may shift from Starbucks or Dutch Bros to Dunkin due to the value bundle and improved order predictability.
Franchisees will monitor store-level economics closely and may opt out of the discount if contribution margins deteriorate.
content.rationale: The $1 discount bundle leverages Dunkin's value positioning and app capabilities to attract time-sensitive breakfast customers who might otherwise try Starbucks' capacity-aware mobile ordering. Allocating most of the budget to labor addresses the need for predictable and fast order fulfillment, which is critical to prevent customer abandonment and competitor switching. Targeted marketing supports repeat usage to build a sustainable basket. The stop rule protects franchisees from unprofitable promotions, consistent with prior concerns about traffic without profitable food attachment.
resource_commitments: $12,000/month for incremental morning labor costs across 15 stores in February 2027
$8,000/month for targeted local app advertising and promotional incentives
Offer a $1 discount on a coffee-and-food breakfast bundle via the Dunkin app during 7-10 a.m. weekdays

actions: Continue to allocate $15,000/month for incremental morning labor at 12 shops near Starbucks pilot cafés.
Continue to allocate $15,000/month for geo-targeted $1 Order Ahead app offer for new/lapsed users at 12 shops near Starbucks pilot cafés.
expected_responses: Starbucks will likely continue to focus on its internal pilot metrics and observe the effects of its capacity reservation policy. They may notice some shifts in market share but are unlikely to alter their pre-planned pilot strategy in February.

Dunkin will continue to monitor the performance of its $6 breakfast Meal Deal. If they observe a significant shift in morning traffic towards drive-through competitors, they might consider adjusting their own offers or service, but their primary focus remains on their value and food proposition.
content.rationale: Starbucks' capacity reservation policy remains in effect for February 2027, creating an ongoing opportunity to capture customers experiencing delays or abandonment. Our initial actions in January were designed to capitalize on this by improving service speed and attracting new users to our convenient drive-through and Order Ahead options. Without new data from January to suggest a change is necessary, continuing this consistent and coherent strategy for February allows us to maintain momentum, reinforce our service proposition, and gather more observations on customer behavior. This approach directly supports our incentives to turn frustrated morning demand into repeat visits and ensure existing-shop growth is durable.
resource_commitments: Allocate $15,000 for incremental morning labor for February 2027.
Allocate $15,000 for geo-targeted $1 Order Ahead app offers for new/lapsed users for February 2027.

actions: Continue the 20% peak café capacity reservation and mobile order admission limits in the 50 pilot cafés through February 2027, maintaining the current weekday 07:00–10:00 window.

Within the pilot, begin a controlled test in 10 of the 50 cafés: dynamically release any unused reserved café capacity to mobile orders if, after the first 60 minutes of peak, café demand is tracking below the 20% allocation (e.g., if less than 15% of capacity has actually been used for café orders by 08:00, release half of the remaining reserved slots for mobile pickup for the rest of the peak window).
expected_responses: Dutch Bros and Dunkin are likely to continue their current promotional tactics, as Starbucks has not signaled a major policy shift or price response. They may monitor for any indication that mobile order reliability improves or worsens.
If the dynamic release test is successful, competitors may eventually copy or counter-message around digital convenience, but within this round, no immediate escalation is expected.

Some habitual mobile customers may experience improved slot availability in the 10 test cafés, potentially reducing abandonment or competitive defection; café customers should not experience increased wait times if the release rule is triggered only when café demand is low.
content.rationale: Maintaining the original reservation policy is necessary to gather enough paired-store and customer repeat data to evaluate the effect on wait times and contribution, as required by the round-two decision rules. However, early evidence may reveal that the 20% café reservation is not fully utilized in some cafés or time intervals, risking unnecessary lost mobile transactions. Dynamically releasing unused reserved capacity in a subset of cafés allows us to test if we can recapture mobile volume without harming the café experience, while still observing the impact on both channels. This approach aligns with the incentive to defend transaction momentum and all-channel contribution, while remaining within staffing and scope constraints.
resource_commitments: Continue incremental staffing (up to 2 additional peak staff-hours per weekday) in all 50 pilot cafés.
Allocate digital and ops resources to implement and monitor the dynamic release rule in 10 pilot cafés (no new budget, but requires coordination and instrumentation updates).

rebuttals.argument: This ruling accurately reflects the different motivations and choices of our various customer segments—habitual app users, café visitors, and time-pressed commuters—based on their experiences in January.
We see the new breakfast bundle offer from Dunkin' in the market. We will evaluate it based on our individual needs for convenience, taste, and price on any given morning.
The continuation of the Dutch Bros Order Ahead offer is noted. For those of us who have switched or are considering it, this remains an attractive option, especially when we're in a hurry.

We don't know the internal rules Starbucks uses, but we will experience the results. We will continue to check the app for pickup times and observe the wait times in the café, and make our daily decisions based on that.

The ruling accurately reflects the dossier facts about buyer behavior in response to mobile order delays and competitor offers, consistent with documented assumptions about habitual app users, café visitors, and commuters.

The ruling correctly states Dunkin's committed actions for February 2027, including the $1 discount bundle launch at 15 franchise stores, budget allocations for labor and advertising, and the stop rule for contribution margin monitoring, all supported by Dunkin dossier facts.

This ruling describes customer behavior that aligns with our strategic objective to capture frustrated morning demand. The diversion of habitual Starbucks app users to competitor mobile apps, particularly those with $1 offers, directly supports the efficacy of our ongoing geo-targeted $1 Order Ahead app offer. The increased readiness of commuters to divert also plays into our drive-through convenience model.

We are continuing our commitment to allocate $15,000/month for incremental morning labor and $15,000/month for geo-targeted $1 Order Ahead app offers for new/lapsed users at our 12 shops near Starbucks pilot cafés. This aligns with our strategy to turn frustrated morning demand into repeat visits while protecting our service proposition, as supported by our capabilities and budget (d.dutch.d5, d.dutch.d6, d.dutch.d7).

The described buyer behaviors—diversion of habitual app users after repeated mobile delays, reinforcement of in-store café visits, and commuter diversion on lateness risk—are consistent with the simulation assumptions and do not conflict with Starbucks' known dossier facts or scenario constraints.

The continued 20% peak café reservation and mobile order admission limits across all 50 pilot cafés, along with the controlled test of dynamic release in 10 cafés, are within the allowed scope, staffing, and measurement constraints specified in the Starbucks dossier.

chain.claim: Habitual Starbucks app users who experienced >8 minute delays at pilot stores in January will divert to competitor mobile apps (notably Dutch Bros $1 Order Ahead or Dunkin's $1 bundle) at the start of February; their return to Starbucks depends on the competitor's service quality.

In-store café visitors at pilot Starbucks locations, having experienced improved and more predictable wait times in January, will reinforce this behavior by choosing these locations more frequently for occasions valuing a reliable in-store experience.
Time-pressed commuters will continue to check the Starbucks app but will more readily divert to Dutch Bros or Dunkin’ if the quoted pickup time risks lateness.
